stories.title: Building a Home for African Stories
stories.excerpt: An evolving look at the vision behind Capital Film & Creatives Village and the environment being created for African storytellers.
stories.content:
## The Baobab Tree That Remembered
In the heart of a small African village called Umoya, where the golden sun painted the earth each morning and the wind carried the songs of distant birds, stood an ancient baobab tree. Its trunk was so wide that ten grown men could barely surround it with their arms.
The elders believed the tree held the memories of everyone who had ever lived in the village. Beneath its branches, generations had gathered to settle disputes, celebrate marriages, and share stories beneath the stars.
Among the villagers lived a curious sixteen-year-old girl named Amara. Unlike most children, who dreamed of leaving the village for the bright lights of the city, Amara wanted to understand the secrets of her homeland.
One evening, while gathering firewood, she heard a faint whisper coming from the baobab tree.
“Amara,” the voice called. “The river is dying, and soon your people will forget who they are.”
Startled, she placed her hand against the rough bark. Suddenly, visions filled her mind: rivers flowing freely, farmers cultivating rich soil, children dancing at festivals, and elders teaching the young the wisdom of their ancestors. Then she saw a different future—dry land, abandoned farms, and a village whose people had forgotten their traditions.
The tree explained that a new road being built nearby would divert the stream that nourished the village. If nobody acted, the community would lose its water supply.
The following morning, Amara gathered the village children and shared what she had witnessed. At first, the adults laughed, dismissing her words as childish imagination. But Amara refused to give up. She convinced the young people to investigate the construction site, where they discovered that the river's natural course had indeed been blocked.
Together, the villagers confronted the builders and negotiated a solution that protected the waterway while allowing construction to continue.
Months later, the river flowed freely again.
At the next village festival, the elders honored Amara beneath the ancient baobab tree.
### She finally understood its greatest secret: Africa's future would not be saved by remembering the past alone, but by having the courage to protect what mattered in the present.
And from that day onward, the people of Umoya taught their children that even the smallest voice could awaken an entire generation.

journalEntries.title: Building the Future of African Storytelling
journalEntries.excerpt: Notes, updates and reflections from the continuing development of Capital Film & Creatives Village.
journalEntries.content:
**Kito thought carefully**. “I learned that courage means continuing when the road is difficult. I learned that kindness matters even when nobody rewards you. And I learned that helping others sometimes makes the journey more meaningful than reaching the destination.”
Suddenly, the silver leaves began to shine brighter. A gentle breeze lifted Kito's face toward the sky, and for one extraordinary moment, the moon appeared so close that he felt its cool light resting in his palms.
He understood then that he had never needed to own the moon to experience its wonder.
When Kito returned home, he became a teacher, sharing stories of his journey with the village children. He taught them to dream boldly, travel bravely, and treat every living thing with compassion.

founderQuotes.text: We are not just building a studio. We are building a home for African stories to finally be told on their own terms.
Technology has caught up with our stories. Now we need the place, and the people, to tell them at a world-class level.
Every filmmaker, journalist and creator who walks through this Village should leave more capable than they arrived.
